8f3989339145fde6a96e3e9e40864516ecae181f.summary: Blog post by Matt Graeber, published 2017-12-22, describing code signing attacks in which an attacker clones a legitimate Microsoft certificate chain and trusts the cloned root on victim systems, so malicious code appears Microsoft-signed. It explains why signature validation accepts such chains, how root CA installation can be detected with Sysmon, how per-user root trust can be restricted through a registry setting, and how root trust can be checked against the authroot.stl list. It also names the Microsoft flight root as a possible cloning candidate.

hedges: The report says the cloned chain passes validation checks, so signature tools will likely be fooled, and the Microsoft flight chain may be a more viable candidate for cloning.
The report calls its registry prevention 'not the most robust' and says there may not be strong preventative mitigations for certificate installation by an admin.
The report says it leaves discussion of further anomalies in the cloned chain and signed code for another blog post.

8f336de69d213b62b8a2a59cb441646e99310ec1.summary: A SANS Internet Storm Center diary entry by Didier Stevens analyses a packet capture containing Cobalt Strike traffic. The author filters HTTP URIs for patterns typical of Cobalt Strike shellcode, notes that the followed stream looks encoded and may use XOR encoding, exports the data, and runs it through a Cobalt Strike beacon analysis tool. The result is the configuration of a beacon. The entry gives no threat actor, victim sector, country or CVE.

8fb41a6db4044de0619582b12dbb6bb3627e50db.summary: A 2021 Medium blog post by Michael Koczwara analyses a PowerShell payload identified as Cobalt Strike, which the author spotted via a tweet. The post says a Base64 block is XOR-encoded and that it can be decrypted with CyberChef after extracting the encoded payload from the PowerShell script. The report names no threat actor, sector, country, CVE or victim.

8f513eb3c4f32592cee418d14747b2097e317b54.summary: A GitHub repository page for deICEr, a small Go tool described as a crude config extractor for IcedID second-stage loaders. The page is mostly repository navigation, file names, commit history and license details. It contains no threat findings, actors, attack dates or campaign details, so it is a tool listing rather than a threat report.
